T. J. Hileman · Glacier National Park Archives, 1938

Mount Gould, 1938. The camera is on the summit; below it the floor of the basin is ice, and there is no lake. 4 photographs were made from this one place between 1938 and 2009 — 71 years.

Scroll through them. The gaps are uneven — 43, 17 and 11 years — and by 2009 the floor of the basin is water with ice floating on it. The rail top left is where you are in the 71 years.

Where this is. Glacier National Park, on the crest of the continent, 91 kilometres across at its widest. The basin you have been looking at is one cirque inside it.

Closer. Grinnell Glacier's own outline is 1.5 km across — 1.6% of the park's width — and the summit all 4 photographs were taken from stands 1.2 km away, on the ridge above it.

Is one basin having a bad century? The world's reference glaciers answer that: cumulative mass balance, 1956 to 2023, 53 glaciers measured in the last year. The average one is 29.7 metres of water thinner than when the record opened.

The stretch the photographs cover, lifted: between 1981 and 2009 — the second frame and the last — the reference glaciers lost 11.6 metres. The first photograph, 1938, is 18 years older than the record.

Now both axes close on the last 25 years. 1998 to 2023: 7.15 metres per decade, against 2.47 over the record's first 25. 2.9 times faster — and a rate is the one thing 4 photographs, however clear, cannot show you.
